section_summaries.epidemiology: Paracoccidioidomycosis is endemic in humid tropical and subtropical areas of Latin America, from Southern Mexico to 34° south in Argentina and Uruguay, with 80% of all patients detected in Brazil, where it is a leading cause of death. It also occurs in Argentina, Colombia, Ecuador, Paraguay, and Venezuela. P. lutzii is endemic only in the west-central regions of Brazil. The incidence and prevalence are not known due to lack of compulsory reporting. Endemic zones have acidic soils, rich in organic material, with many streams and rivers, and exuberant vegetation. The habitat of Paracoccidioides spp. is not well known but probably lives in soil near water. Animal-to-human and human-to-human transmission has not been confirmed. Reactivation of latent pulmonary or extrapulmonary foci leading to progressive clinical forms is frequently observed in adult males older than 35 years of age, especially rural workers. Genetics, smoking, and alcoholism are considered risk factors. The juvenile type is less common (3%-5% of clinical cases), affects both sexes equally, and has an acute or subacute course.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: In infected tissue and culture at 37°C, Paracoccidioides spp. appear as spherical cells of 10-40 µm with a thick birefringent cell wall and several peripheral buds, like a pilot wheel. Infection is most likely acquired by airborne inhalation of aleurioconidiae that turn into yeast-like elements inside alveolar macrophages. An initial non-specific inflammatory reaction progresses to epithelioid cell granuloma with giant cells, plasmacytes, and lymphocytes. Microabscesses and caseous necrosis are common, followed by tissue repair involving fibrosis. Cell-mediated immunity, with a predominant Th1 cytokine response, is the most important defense mechanism and is genetically controlled. Antibodies are produced during progressive disease, but their significance is not well understood. Patients with severe disease show increased activity of regulatory T cells with strong immune suppression produced by IL10 and TGF-β. Progressive paracoccidioidomycosis may result from reactivation of a latent focus of infection (in chronic forms) or lack of control of the primary infection (in the acute juvenile type).
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: Primary infections are often asymptomatic or mild and self-limited; symptomatic primary infections are rare, with 6%-50% of inhabitants in endemic regions having positive paracoccidioidin skin tests. The acute form of juvenile type in children and adolescents has an acute course with toxemia, fever, asthenia, anorexia, weight loss, subcutaneous abscesses, diffuse lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, diarrhea, jaundice, anemia, and leukocytosis with eosinophilia, likely due to immune response failure. Acneiform lesions, scrofuloderma, osteomyelitis, and gastrointestinal involvement are common. The chronic form of adult type, usually in adult males, has an insidious onset with asthenia, weight loss, and exertional dyspnea. Pulmonary involvement occurs in 25% of cases, presenting with low-grade fever, cough, mucopurulent sputum, hemoptysis, and dyspnea. Chest x-rays show bilateral symmetric lesions, often perihilar, resembling butterfly wings, with infiltrates, micronodular and linear shadows. Death can occur after several years due to cachexia or respiratory impairments. Multifocal presentation is seen in over 70% of patients, involving skin, mucous membranes, lungs, lymph nodes, adrenal glands, abdominal organs, and the central nervous system (CNS). Typical oropharyngeal lesions are ulcers with hemorrhagic granulomatous foci and an infiltrated hard base (mulberry-like stomatitis), with firm, red-violet edema often on lips and gingival mucosa. Laryngeal attacks cause dysphonia, obstructive dyspnea, and dysphagia. Skin lesions include papules, nodules, and ulcers, often on the face and neck; some become vegetative and papillomatous. Cervical lymph nodes are often hypertrophic and firm, potentially suppurative or necrotic, forming scrofula-like lesions. Adrenal gland involvement occurs in >15% of chronic cases, causing Addison's disease when severe. CNS compromise occurs in 10% of cases, with abscessed granulomas and subacute meningoencephalitis. Other locations include testicles, epididymis, prostate, bones, liver, and spleen. Death may result from respiratory failure, malnutrition, or intercurrent infections. In some Brazilian states, a different clinical form with chronic peritonitis, hepatosplenomegaly, mesenteric lymphadenopathy, and digestive tract compromise is observed, probably related to P. lutzii. After effective treatment, lesions can remain latent, and relapses may occur. AIDS-related paracoccidioidomycosis is frequently observed only in Brazil, typically presenting as acute disseminated juvenile type or severe disseminated chronic form, with a ~30% mortality rate in treated cases. Co-infection with tuberculosis is detected in 10%-12% of cases. The incidence of neoplasms, especially lung cancer, seems more common among paracoccidioidomycosis patients.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Diagnosis is confirmed by finding typical yeastlike elements of Paracoccidioides spp. in microscopy of wet preparations. Cultures should be performed on yeast extract agar without glucose, brain-heart infusion agar, and Sabouraud dextrose agar with antibiotics and cycloheximide, incubated for 4 weeks at 25°C and 37°C. The fungus grows slowly, and its isolation is difficult. Histopathologic specimens should be stained with periodic acid-Schiff or Grocott methenamine-silver. In progressive forms, antibodies can be detected by immunodiffusion, counterimmunoelectrophoresis, complement fixation tests, and ELISA, utilizing specific glycoprotein of 43 kDa (gp 43) or other antigens. Western blot is infrequently used. Antibody titers are proportional to disease severity and decline with cure. For P. lutzii in endemic areas, serologic reactions require species-specific antigens. In severe cases, antigen detection in serum and urine via ELISA using monoclonal antibodies against gp 43 is possible. The paracoccidioidin skin test has limited diagnostic value for progressive disease but is useful in epidemiologic studies. Patients with severe disease often show positive serology with high titers, negative paracoccidioidin skin test, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia, eosinophilia, and low CD4-positive T-cell counts; these changes may normalize with clinical improvement. The differential diagnosis for chronic disseminated disease includes tuberculosis, histoplasmosis, leishmaniasis, carcinoma, and sarcoidosis. Acute disseminated disease resembles tuberculosis, malaria, leukemia, and lymphomas.
section_summaries.treatment: Sulfonamides, ketoconazole, itraconazole, fluconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, and amphotericin B have been successfully used. Accepted treatment schedules include ketoconazole 200-400 mg/day for 12 months, itraconazole 100-200 mg/day for 6 months, and intravenous amphotericin B 0.7-0.8 mg/kg daily up to a maximum total dose of 35 mg/kg. Itraconazole is the treatment of choice (over 95% effective) but not for CNS infection, and its absorption requires gastric acid, being reduced by fungal involvement of mesenteric lymph nodes and digestive tract, or when co-administered with rifampin. Amphotericin B is indicated for severe cases with malabsorption. Fluconazole (oral or IV, 800 mg daily) is used for brain lesions. Co-trimoxazole is still frequently used in Brazil for newly diagnosed patients, chronic unifocal progressive disease, and maintenance after amphotericin B. Dosage is 160 mg trimethoprim and 800 mg sulfamethoxazole every 12 hours for 2-3 years, with higher doses for CNS involvement. Children are usually treated with intravenous amphotericin B (0.7 mg/kg daily) or oral sulfadiazine (200 mg/kg/day). Other drugs like voriconazole, posaconazole, and terbinafine have limited clinical experience; voriconazole is similarly efficacious to itraconazole but more expensive. Treatment is prolonged, relapses are common, and incapacitating sequelae like laryngeal/tracheal stenosis, buccal atresia, and pulmonary fibrosis often occur. In murine models, simultaneous administration of itraconazole and pentoxifylline reduced pulmonary fibrosis.
section_summaries.prevention: Although several antigens have been studied as immunogens to prevent paracoccidioidomycosis in laboratory animals, none of them have been used in human beings, and there is no measure to avoid the risk of infection.
